Part 0

How to use this notebook

Read it in order once. Every part builds on the one before it, the same way our code is built in layers.

This notebook explains our project from the ground up. You do not need any background in cryptography. When a new word appears it is explained right there, and the glossary at the end collects all of them.

What our project is, in three sentences

Quantum computers will one day break the encryption the internet uses today (RSA and elliptic curves). NIST has standardized a replacement called ML-KEM (published as FIPS 203 in August 2024), which is built on a lattice math problem that quantum computers are not known to solve. We implemented ML-KEM ourselves in Python straight from the FIPS 203 document, proved it is correct with NIST's official test vectors, and benchmarked it against RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography on our own laptop.

Panel questions

opening questions

  1. We studied ML-KEM, the post-quantum key-exchange standard NIST published as FIPS 203 in 2024. We implemented it from scratch in Python by following the standard line by line, proved it matches the standard byte for byte using 240 of NIST's official test vectors, checked it works with two professional implementations (liboqs and OpenSSL), and benchmarked it against RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. ML-KEM turned out much faster than RSA and faster than NIST elliptic curves at the same security level, but its keys and ciphertexts are much larger.

  2. To understand it. Writing every algorithm ourselves forced us to learn every step of the standard, and it gave us a readable reference that maps line by line to FIPS 203. For the speed comparison we used professional C libraries (liboqs and OpenSSL), because comparing slow Python against fast C would be unfair.

  3. A US federal standard from NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) titled "Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard". It was published on 13 August 2024 and defines ML-KEM exactly: the algorithms, the parameter sets and the byte formats.

  4. ML-KEM is the standardized version of CRYSTALS-Kyber, the scheme NIST selected in 2022. They are very close but not byte-compatible: FIPS 203 changed a few details (for example, it adds the parameter k into a hash as domain separation, and it derives the shared key differently). Our code implements final FIPS 203, which is why it passes NIST's FIPS 203 test vectors.

Part 1

Why post-quantum cryptography

What problem ML-KEM solves, and why the world is switching to it now.

1.1 Two kinds of encryption

Symmetric encryption (for example AES) uses one shared secret key for both locking and unlocking. It is very fast and is used to encrypt almost all real data. Its problem: both sides must already share the key.

Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography uses a key pair: a public key anyone may see, and a private key only the owner keeps. It solves the key-sharing problem, but it is much slower. So real systems combine the two:

  1. Use public-key cryptography once, at the start, to agree on a fresh random secret.
  2. Use that secret as the AES key for all the actual data.

Step 1 is called key exchange or key establishment. It happens every time your browser opens an HTTPS connection. ML-KEM replaces this step.

1.2 What a KEM is

A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is a way to do key exchange with exactly three algorithms:

AlgorithmWho runs itInputOutput
KeyGenBob (receiver)randomnessencapsulation key ek (public), decapsulation key dk (secret)
EncapsAlice (sender)Bob's ekshared key K and ciphertext c
DecapsBobhis dk and Alice's cthe same shared key K
Key idea

A KEM does not encrypt your message. It only creates and delivers a random 32-byte secret key. The message itself is then encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM using that key. Our demo shows exactly this.

1.3 How RSA and elliptic curves do it today

RSA is secure because factoring a huge number N = p × q (two secret primes) is hard. For key exchange, the sender encrypts a random key with the receiver's public key (RSA-OAEP); only the private key can decrypt it.

Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), for example X25519 or NIST P-256, is secure because the discrete logarithm problem on an elliptic curve is hard. Both sides combine their own private key with the other's public key (Diffie-Hellman) and land on the same shared point. ECC keys are tiny (32 bytes for X25519) and fast, which is why ECC dominates today's internet.

1.4 The quantum threat

In 1994 Peter Shor published Shor's algorithm. On a large enough quantum computer it solves both factoring and discrete logarithms efficiently. That breaks RSA and ECC completely; making keys bigger does not help, because the attack scales too well.

Quantum computers affect symmetric crypto much less. Grover's algorithm speeds up brute-force search only by a square root, so AES-256 keeps about 128-bit security. That is still safe.

SchemeHard problemClassical computerQuantum computer
RSAinteger factoringsecurebroken (Shor)
ECC (ECDH)elliptic-curve discrete logsecurebroken (Shor)
AES-256brute-force key searchsecurestill secure (Grover only halves the bits)
ML-KEMModule Learning With Errors (lattices)secureno known efficient attack

1.5 Why switch now, before quantum computers exist

"Harvest now, decrypt later." An attacker can record encrypted traffic today and store it. When a large quantum computer becomes available, maybe years from now, they decrypt the recorded key exchanges and read everything. Data that must stay secret for 10+ years (medical, government, financial) is already at risk. The key exchange is the part to fix first, because it protects all data sent afterwards.

1.6 How ML-KEM became the standard

DateEvent
2016NIST opens a public competition for post-quantum algorithms (69 complete submissions in round 1).
2017–2022Three rounds of public analysis by cryptographers worldwide.
July 2022NIST selects CRYSTALS-Kyber as the key-establishment standard.
Aug 2023Draft FIPS 203 published for public comment.
13 Aug 2024Final FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) published, alongside FIPS 204 (ML-DSA signatures) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA signatures).

It is already deployed. Chrome, Firefox and Cloudflare use the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange in TLS, Signal's PQXDH protocol and Apple's iMessage PQ3 use Kyber, and OpenSSL 3.5+ ships ML-KEM. (Our benchmarks even used OpenSSL 4.0's ML-KEM.)

RSA and ECC rely on factoring and discrete logs, which Shor's algorithm breaks on a quantum computer. ML-KEM relies on a lattice problem with no known quantum shortcut, and because attackers can store today's traffic and decrypt it later, the key exchange has to be replaced now.

Panel questions

Part 1

  1. Public-key encryption lets you encrypt any message you choose. A KEM does not take a message: Encaps generates a random key itself and returns it together with a ciphertext that delivers it. It is a narrower tool made exactly for key exchange, and it is simpler to make secure. The real data is then encrypted with a symmetric cipher using that key.

  2. It efficiently solves integer factoring and discrete logarithms (including on elliptic curves). RSA depends on factoring and ECC/Diffie-Hellman depend on discrete logs, so both are broken. It does not help against the lattice problem that ML-KEM uses.

  3. No. Grover gives only a square-root speed-up for brute-force search, so a 256-bit key behaves like a 128-bit key against a quantum attacker. That is still far out of reach. So AES-256 stays; only the public-key part (key exchange and signatures) must change.

  4. Because of "harvest now, decrypt later": encrypted traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. Anything that must stay secret for many years is already exposed. Migrating large systems also takes a decade or more.

  5. ML stands for Module-Lattice. Its security rests on the Module Learning With Errors (Module-LWE) problem, a problem about lattices. Part 3 explains it.

  6. Yes. Hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 is enabled by default in Chrome and Firefox and supported by Cloudflare for TLS; Signal (PQXDH) and Apple iMessage (PQ3) use Kyber; OpenSSL 3.5 and later include ML-KEM.

  7. Running a classical exchange (like X25519) and ML-KEM together and combining both secrets. The connection stays safe as long as either one is unbroken. It protects against a future quantum computer and also against any undiscovered weakness in the newer ML-KEM. We discuss hybrids but did not implement one.

Part 2

The math, from zero

Four ideas are enough: remainders, polynomials, the special ring ML-KEM lives in, and vectors of polynomials.

2.1 Modular arithmetic ("clock arithmetic")

On a 12-hour clock, 5 hours after 10 o'clock is 3 o'clock, not 15. That is arithmetic modulo 12: after every operation you keep only the remainder after dividing by 12.

15 mod 12 = 3 (15 = 1·12 + 3) 7 × 5 = 35, 35 mod 12 = 11 3 − 5 = −2, −2 mod 12 = 10 (add 12 until it is in 0…11)

ML-KEM does everything modulo q = 3329. Every number is kept in the range 0 … 3328. The set of these numbers is written Z_q ("integers mod q"). Because 3329 is a prime, every non-zero number has a multiplicative inverse (you can "divide"), which the NTT needs.

Centered representatives. Sometimes it is easier to think of numbers near q as small negatives: 3328 is "−1", 3327 is "−2". We write x mod± q for the version in −1664 … 1664. "Small noise" in ML-KEM means numbers whose centered value is close to 0.

2.2 Polynomials as lists of numbers

A polynomial like 3 + 2X + 5X² is just a list of coefficients [3, 2, 5]. You add polynomials coefficient by coefficient. You multiply them like in school, collecting powers of X. In ML-KEM every polynomial has exactly 256 coefficients (degree up to 255), each in Z_q. In our code a polynomial is simply a Python list of 256 integers.

2.3 The ring Rq = Zq[X]/(X²⁵⁶ + 1)

Multiplying two degree-255 polynomials gives degree up to 510, which is too long. ML-KEM keeps every result at 256 coefficients using one rule:

X²⁵⁶ = −1 (so X²⁵⁷ = −X, X²⁵⁸ = −X², …)

Any coefficient that lands at position 256 or higher wraps around to the start with its sign flipped. This is called negacyclic wrapping. A tiny example with only 4 coefficients (X⁴ = −1) and q = 17:

(1 + 2X) · (3 + X³) = 3 + X³ + 6X + 2X⁴ school multiplication = 3 + 6X + X³ + 2·(−1) replace X⁴ by −1 = 1 + 6X + 0X² + 1X³ → [1, 6, 0, 1] (all mod 17)

This is exactly what our reference function schoolbook_mul in tests/test_ntt.py does for 256 coefficients: c[i] − c[i+256].

Key idea

Rq is "polynomials with 256 coefficients mod 3329, where X²⁵⁶ wraps to −1". Every secret, key and ciphertext in ML-KEM is built from elements of this ring.

2.4 Vectors and matrices of polynomials: "modules"

Instead of vectors of numbers, ML-KEM uses vectors whose entries are polynomials. A vector of k polynomials is written R_q^k; a k×k matrix of polynomials is R_q^(k×k). The number k (2, 3 or 4) is the "module rank" and is the main security dial: ML-KEM-512 uses k = 2, ML-KEM-768 uses k = 3, ML-KEM-1024 uses k = 4.

Matrix-vector multiplication works exactly as usual, except each "multiply" is a polynomial multiplication in Rq and each "add" is polynomial addition:

(A·s)[i] = A[i][0]·s[0] + A[i][1]·s[1] + … + A[i][k−1]·s[k−1]

In our code this is mat_vec_mul_ntt in src/mlkem/ntt.py. The "inner product" tᵀ·y (one polynomial) is inner_ntt.

2.5 Bits, bytes and "little-endian"

FIPS 203 stores bits least-significant first inside each byte: byte 0x01 is the bit list [1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]. Getting this backwards is the most common implementation bug, and our test test_bytes_to_bits_lsb_first checks it.

2.6 Randomness

Secure randomness must come from a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG). Our public functions use os.urandom, which asks the operating system. Python's random module is predictable and must never be used for keys; we use it only in tests, where predictability is useful.

Panel questions

Part 2

  1. With a prime modulus, every non-zero number has a multiplicative inverse, so Z_q is a field. The NTT needs inverses (for example 128⁻¹ mod q = 3303 when undoing the transform) and needs roots of unity to exist, which is guaranteed by q being prime with 256 dividing q − 1.

  2. It sets the rule X²⁵⁶ = −1, so every product is folded back to 256 coefficients with a sign flip on the part that wraps around. This keeps all objects a fixed size and gives the ring the structure the NTT can exploit.

  3. A vector of ring elements, here a vector of k polynomials. It sits between plain LWE (vectors of numbers, very large keys) and Ring-LWE (a single polynomial, very structured). Modules let NIST change security just by changing k (2, 3, 4) while reusing the same 256-coefficient polynomial code.

  4. Writing a number mod q in the range −(q−1)/2 … (q−1)/2 instead of 0 … q−1. For example 3328 is −1. It is how we measure whether noise is "small": we look at how far the centered value is from 0.

  5. os.urandom is a cryptographically secure generator from the operating system. Python's random is a Mersenne Twister, which is predictable once you see enough output. Keys made with it could be recovered. We use random only inside tests to get reproducible inputs.

Part 3

Lattices and Learning With Errors

The hard problem that makes ML-KEM secure, explained with a toy example you can check by hand.

3.1 Solving equations is easy

Suppose I pick a secret vector s = (2, 3) and show you some equations mod 17:

3·s₀ + 5·s₁ = 4 (mod 17) 7·s₀ + 2·s₁ = 3 (mod 17) 11·s₀ + 4·s₁ = 0 (mod 17)

You can recover s with ordinary Gaussian elimination, the method from school. Even with thousands of unknowns, a computer does this instantly. In matrix form this is b = A·s, and it gives no security at all.

3.2 Add a little noise and it becomes hard

Now I add a small random error e = (1, −1, 0) to each right-hand side before showing it to you:

3·s₀ + 5·s₁ ≈ 5 (true value 4, plus 1) 7·s₀ + 2·s₁ ≈ 2 (true value 3, minus 1) 11·s₀ + 4·s₁ ≈ 0 (true value 0, plus 0) b = A·s + e → b = (5, 2, 0)

Gaussian elimination now fails, because the errors get mixed and amplified at every step. With a few hundred unknowns and well-chosen noise, no known algorithm, classical or quantum, recovers s in a reasonable time. This is the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem, introduced by Oded Regev in 2005 (he received the Gödel Prize in 2018 for it).

Key idea

LWE: given a random matrix A and b = A·s + e with small noise e, find s. Easy without the noise, believed hard with it, even for quantum computers.

There is also a decision version: tell whether a pair (A, b) came from A·s + e or is completely random. It is equally hard, and it is the version security proofs use: the public key looks like random numbers to anyone without s.

3.3 Where lattices come in

A lattice is a regular grid of points: every integer combination of some basis vectors. In 2 dimensions it looks like wallpaper; ML-KEM's lattices have hundreds of dimensions.

Regev proved that solving LWE on average is at least as hard as solving certain lattice problems (like finding short vectors) in the worst case. So breaking random LWE instances would mean solving every instance of a problem mathematicians have attacked for decades. The best known attacks (lattice reduction algorithms such as BKZ and lattice sieving) take time exponential in the dimension, and quantum computers give only small speed-ups against them.

3.4 From LWE to Ring-LWE to Module-LWE

VariantThe "A·s + e" usesProsCons
LWEa big matrix of numberssimplest, most conservativepublic keys of hundreds of kilobytes
Ring-LWEsingle polynomials in Rqsmall keys, fast (NTT)a lot of algebraic structure; fixed security levels
Module-LWE (ML-KEM)a k×k matrix of polynomialssmall keys, fast, less structure; change security by changing kslightly bigger than Ring-LWE

One polynomial multiplication in Rq behaves like multiplying by a special 256×256 matrix. So a k×k matrix of polynomials is a compact way to describe a large (256k)×(256k) LWE matrix. ML-KEM-768 (k = 3) is effectively an LWE problem in dimension 768, which is where the name comes from.

3.5 Where this shows up in our code

In src/mlkem/kpke.py, keygen computes exactly one Module-LWE sample:

t_hat = vec_add(mat_vec_mul_ntt(A_hat, s_hat), e_hat)  # t = A s + e: an MLWE sample

The public key contains t and the seed for A. Recovering the secret s from them is Module-LWE.

The public key is A times the secret plus small noise. Without the noise, you could solve for the secret with Gaussian elimination. With the noise, it becomes the Module-LWE problem, which reduces to hard lattice problems that have no known efficient quantum algorithm.

Panel questions

Part 3

  1. Given a uniformly random matrix A (mod q) and b = A·s + e, where s is a secret vector and e is a vector of small random errors, find s (search-LWE), or tell (A, b) apart from uniformly random (decision-LWE).

  2. Every elimination step combines equations, which also adds and multiplies their errors. After a few steps the accumulated error is as large as q, so the results are meaningless. Without errors it would work instantly.

  3. The set of all integer combinations of some basis vectors: a regular, infinite grid of points in n-dimensional space. Hard lattice problems include finding the shortest non-zero vector (SVP) or the lattice point closest to a given target (CVP).

  4. The set of values A·s (mod q) forms a lattice. The public value b is a point near one lattice point (off by the small error e). Recovering s means finding that closest lattice point, a CVP-type problem. Regev showed average-case LWE is at least as hard as worst-case lattice problems (quantumly; later work gave classical reductions for some parameters).

  5. Plain LWE needs huge keys. Ring-LWE is compact but very structured, and changing security means changing the ring. Module-LWE keeps the compact polynomial arithmetic and fast NTT, has less structure, and lets NIST set three security levels just by choosing k = 2, 3 or 4.

  6. Lattice reduction (BKZ) using lattice sieving as a subroutine. Their cost grows exponentially with the dimension. Known quantum algorithms give only a modest improvement to sieving (a smaller exponent), not the exponential collapse that Shor gives for RSA. NIST's parameter sets include margin for this. Member A covers exact estimates with the lattice estimator.

  7. Zero noise makes the problem easy (plain linear algebra). Noise too large would stop the legitimate receiver from decrypting, because decryption has to round the noise away. ML-KEM picks noise just large enough for security and small enough that decryption practically never fails.

Part 4

The building blocks

Hash functions, byte encoding, compression and sampling: the low-level tools every higher layer uses.

4.1 Hash functions and the XOF (src/mlkem/hashes.py)

A hash function turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint that looks random. Changing one input bit changes about half the output bits, and you cannot run it backwards. ML-KEM uses the SHA-3 family (FIPS 202, based on the Keccak "sponge"). An XOF (extendable-output function) is a hash that can produce as many output bytes as you ask for.

Name in FIPS 203Built fromOutputUsed for
H(s)SHA3-25632 Bfingerprint of the public key, H(ek)
J(s)SHAKE25632 Bthe "fake" key on rejection, J(z ‖ c)
G(c)SHA3-512, split in two2 × 32 Bderive two seeds at once: (ρ, σ) and (K, r)
PRF_η(s, b)SHAKE25664η Brandom bytes for the noise polynomials
XOF(ρ, i, j)SHAKE128as neededrandom bytes for the public matrix A

Our code calls Python's built-in hashlib. One detail: hashlib's SHAKE cannot "stream", so XOF asks for n bytes, and SampleNTT asks again with a larger n if it runs out. This is safe because the first n bytes of a longer output are always the same as a shorter output. We test this retry path on purpose.

4.2 Turning numbers into bytes (src/mlkem/encoding.py)

Keys and ciphertexts are polynomials, but networks send bytes. ByteEncoded (Algorithm 5) packs 256 numbers of d bits each into 32·d bytes; ByteDecoded (Algorithm 6) unpacks them.

  • A full coefficient mod 3329 needs 12 bits, so one polynomial takes 256 × 12 / 8 = 384 bytes. That is why sizes in ML-KEM are multiples of 384.
  • For d = 12, decoding reduces each value mod q. A 12-bit value like 4095 decodes to 4095 − 3329 = 766. The encapsulation-key check relies on this.
  • We wrote two versions: byte_encode_ref copies the spec's bit-by-bit loop exactly; byte_encode packs everything into one big Python integer and is much faster. A test checks both produce identical bytes for every d.

4.3 Compression: throwing away bits on purpose

To make ciphertexts smaller, ML-KEM keeps only the top d bits of each coefficient. It maps the range 0…3328 onto 0…2d−1 by rounding:

Compress_d(x) = round( (2^d / q) · x ) mod 2^d Decompress_d(y) = round( (q / 2^d) · y )

Compression loses a little information, like saving a photo at lower quality. The loss acts as a bit of extra noise, which decryption tolerates. Real examples from our code:

xdCompressDecompress backError
1000451040+40
832100closer to 0
833111665closer to q/2
3000100wraps: 3000 is near 3329 ≡ 0

Compress1 is the heart of decryption: it answers "is this number closer to 0 or to q/2 = 1665?" Numbers from 833 to 2496 give 1; the rest give 0.

We use only integer arithmetic (no floating point), which avoids rounding surprises. Our tests check every x in 0…3328 against exact fraction arithmetic, and check that the round-trip error never exceeds round(q / 2^(d+1)).

4.4 Sampling the public matrix: SampleNTT (src/mlkem/sampling.py, Algorithm 7)

The matrix A must look uniformly random mod q, but sending it would be huge. Instead the public key contains a 32-byte seed ρ, and both sides regenerate A from it with SHAKE128. For each entry:

  1. Read 3 bytes from the XOF stream: 24 bits, split into two 12-bit numbers d₁ and d₂ (0…4095).
  2. Keep a number only if it is less than 3329; otherwise throw it away. This is rejection sampling. It keeps the distribution exactly uniform (about 81% of candidates are kept).
  3. Repeat until 256 coefficients are collected.
Common mistake

Entry Â[i][j] is generated from ρ ‖ j ‖ i, with j first. Swapping them silently produces the transpose of A. Round-trip tests still pass, but the result no longer matches FIPS 203. Our test test_gen_matrix_index_order guards this, and the NIST vectors would catch it too.

SampleNTT's output is already in the NTT domain (the Â "hat" notation), so it is never transformed; it is used directly for fast multiplication.

4.5 Sampling small noise: SamplePolyCBD (Algorithm 8)

The secret s and errors e must be small. ML-KEM draws them from the centered binomial distribution CBDη:

take 2η random bits x = (sum of the first η bits) y = (sum of the next η bits) coefficient = x − y ∈ {−η, …, η}

For η = 2 the values −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 appear with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16. For η = 3 they are 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1 out of 64. It looks like a bell curve, approximating the Gaussian noise the LWE theory assumes, but it needs only bit counting: fast and easy to implement in constant time. Our Figure 5 shows our sampler matches these probabilities.

The random bits come from PRF_η(σ, N): the same seed σ with a counter N = 0, 1, 2, … so each polynomial gets fresh, independent bits.

Panel questions

Part 4

  1. Each has a separate job (fingerprinting the key, deriving seeds, generating noise, expanding the matrix, the rejection key). Using distinct functions or inputs for each job ("domain separation") ensures outputs of one job can never be confused with another's. They are all SHA-3/SHAKE underneath.

  2. An extendable-output function produces an arbitrary-length output. SampleNTT does not know in advance how many bytes it needs (rejection sampling throws some away), so it needs a stream of bytes. SHAKE128 is the fastest SHA-3 variant and is sufficient for expanding public randomness.

  3. For ML-KEM-768, A is 3×3 polynomials × 384 bytes = 3,456 bytes. The seed is 32 bytes. Both sides regenerate A deterministically from ρ, so the public key stays small.

  4. We generate 12-bit numbers (0…4095) but need uniform numbers in 0…3328. Taking "x mod 3329" would make small values twice as likely (bias). Instead we discard any value ≥ 3329 and try again. The kept values are exactly uniform.

  5. A coefficient is (sum of η random bits) − (sum of η other random bits), which gives small values in [−η, η] with a bell shape. A true discrete Gaussian needs high-precision sampling that is slow and hard to make constant-time. CBD approximates it well enough for security and needs only bit counting.

  6. It keeps only the top d bits of each ciphertext coefficient (10 or 11 bits for u, 4 or 5 for v), which shrinks the ciphertext. It adds a small rounding error, but decryption already tolerates noise up to q/4, and the parameters were chosen so the total noise stays far below that.

  7. 256 coefficients × 12 bits each (enough for values up to 4095 ≥ 3328) = 3,072 bits = 384 bytes. So ek = 384k + 32 bytes (k polynomials plus the 32-byte seed ρ).

  8. Within each byte, bit 0 (value 1) comes first. FIPS 203 Algorithms 3 and 4 define this order. Reading bits the other way round still round-trips in your own code but produces bytes that don't match the standard or other implementations.

Part 5

The Number-Theoretic Transform

The trick that makes polynomial multiplication fast, and the hardest part of the implementation.

5.1 The problem: multiplication is slow

Multiplying two 256-coefficient polynomials the school way needs 256 × 256 = 65,536 small multiplications. ML-KEM-768 does many of these per operation.

5.2 The idea: change representation

Think of how multiplying numbers is easier with logarithms: convert, do an easy operation, convert back. The NTT does the same for polynomials:

  1. Transform both polynomials with the NTT (fast, about n·log n work).
  2. Multiply piece by piece in the transformed ("NTT") domain. This is cheap.
  3. Transform back with the inverse NTT.

The NTT is the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) done with whole numbers mod q instead of complex numbers. Instead of complex roots of unity it uses a number ζ whose powers "cycle" mod q.

5.3 Why ζ = 17 and q = 3329

An FFT of size 256 needs a primitive 256-th root of unity: a number ζ with ζ²⁵⁶ = 1 but no smaller power equal to 1. That exists mod q only if 256 divides q − 1. For ML-KEM:

q − 1 = 3328 = 256 × 13 ✓ so 256-th roots exist 17¹²⁸ mod 3329 = 3328 = −1 (half-way round) 17²⁵⁶ mod 3329 = 1 (full circle)

But 512 does not divide 3328. A "complete" NTT for X²⁵⁶ + 1 would need a 512-th root of unity. So ML-KEM uses an incomplete NTT: it splits the polynomial into 128 small pieces of degree 1 (pairs of coefficients) instead of 256 single numbers.

5.4 How the split works

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, knowing a polynomial modulo each of the 128 factors is the same as knowing the polynomial. Each level is done with butterflies: for a pair of coefficients (a, b) and a twiddle factor ζ:

forward (Cooley–Tukey, Alg 9): t = ζ·b; a' = a + t; b' = a − t inverse (Gentleman–Sande, Alg 10): a' = a + b; b' = ζ·(b − a); finally × 128⁻¹ = 3303

5.5 Multiplying in the NTT domain (Algorithms 11 and 12)

After the NTT a polynomial is 128 pairs (a₀, a₁), each meaning a₀ + a₁X modulo X² − γ. Multiplying two pairs uses the rule X² = γ:

(a₀ + a₁X)(b₀ + b₁X) = a₀b₀ + (a₀b₁ + a₁b₀)X + a₁b₁X² = (a₀b₀ + a₁b₁γ) + (a₀b₁ + a₁b₀)X since X² = γ

That is base_case_multiply in our code: 5 multiplications per pair, 128 pairs, about 640 multiplications instead of 65,536.

5.6 The precomputed tables

# src/mlkem/ntt.py
ZETAS  = [pow(ZETA, bitrev7(i), Q) for i in range(128)]          # for NTT / NTT^-1
GAMMAS = [pow(ZETA, 2 * bitrev7(i) + 1, Q) for i in range(128)]  # for BaseCaseMultiply
N_INV  = pow(128, -1, Q)                                          # 3303

bitrev7 reverses the 7 bits of the index (the NTT visits factors in bit-reversed order, like the FFT). We compute these tables ourselves and a test compares them against the tables printed in FIPS 203 Appendix A, which we copied from the PDF. For example ZETAS[1] = 17⁶⁴ mod 3329 = 1729.

5.7 How we proved the NTT is right

  • Round trip: ntt_inv(ntt(f)) == f for 100 random polynomials.
  • The decisive test: NTT multiplication equals slow schoolbook multiplication with the X²⁵⁶ = −1 rule, for random inputs. If this passes, the NTT is correct.
  • Edge cases: 1·a = a, and X·X²⁵⁵ = X²⁵⁶ = −1.
  • Linearity: NTT(a + b) = NTT(a) + NTT(b).

Our benchmark bench/ntt_vs_schoolbook.py measured, in pure Python: schoolbook 4.44 ms, full NTT multiply (2 transforms, pointwise product, inverse) 0.42 ms (about 10.5× faster), and pointwise product alone 0.034 ms (about 130×). ML-KEM keeps keys in the NTT domain, so it often pays only the cheap pointwise cost.

Because q − 1 = 3328 is divisible by 256, there is a 256-th root of unity, ζ = 17. That lets us use an FFT-like transform that splits X²⁵⁶ + 1 into 128 quadratic factors, so a polynomial product becomes 128 tiny products. We verified it against schoolbook multiplication.

Panel questions

Part 5

  1. Because 256 divides q − 1 = 3328 = 2⁸ · 13, a primitive 256-th root of unity exists mod q; ζ = 17 is one. That is exactly what a size-256 (negacyclic, incomplete) NTT needs.

  2. A complete NTT of X²⁵⁶ + 1 would need a 512-th root of unity, which does not exist mod 3329 (512 does not divide 3328). So the splitting stops one level early, at 128 quadratic factors X² − γ, and multiplication in the NTT domain works on pairs of coefficients (BaseCaseMultiply).

  3. The basic NTT step on two coefficients: multiply one by a twiddle factor ζ and form the sum and difference. Each NTT layer applies 128 butterflies; there are 7 layers.

  4. Each of the 7 inverse layers doubles the values, a total factor of 2⁷ = 128. Multiplying by 128⁻¹ mod 3329, which is 3303 (since 128 × 3303 ≡ 1 mod 3329), undoes that scaling.

  5. Four checks: our twiddle tables match FIPS 203 Appendix A exactly; NTT then inverse NTT returns the input; NTT-based multiplication equals slow schoolbook multiplication with X²⁵⁶ = −1; and finally all 240 NIST vectors pass, which depend on the NTT.

  6. The in-place FFT/NTT algorithm naturally produces its outputs in bit-reversed index order. FIPS 203 keeps them in that order and indexes the twiddle factors by BitRev₇(i) so everything lines up without an extra reordering pass.

  7. In pure Python, a full NTT-based multiply was about 10.5× faster than schoolbook (0.42 ms vs 4.44 ms), and the pointwise multiply alone was about 130× faster. In C the gap is similar or larger.

  8. The value is stored in the NTT domain. In our code these variables end in _hat. The matrix is generated directly in the NTT domain, and the secret key is stored as ŝ, so most multiplications need no forward transform at all.

Part 6

K-PKE: the inner lock

A simple public-key encryption scheme built on Module-LWE. ML-KEM wraps it, so understand this first.

K-PKE (FIPS 203 Section 5, Algorithms 13–15) encrypts a 32-byte message m, which is 256 bits, one bit per polynomial coefficient. Our code is in src/mlkem/kpke.py.

6.1 Key generation (Algorithm 13)

  1. Start from a 32-byte random seed d. Compute (ρ, σ) = G(d ‖ k): ρ is the public seed, σ the secret seed. Appending k is domain separation, so the same d gives unrelated keys for different parameter sets.
  2. Generate the matrix Â from ρ with SampleNTT.
  3. Sample the secret s and the error e (k small polynomials each) with CBDη1, using PRF(σ, 0…2k−1).
  4. Compute t̂ = Â·ŝ + ê in the NTT domain. This is the Module-LWE sample.
  5. Public key ek = ByteEncode₁₂(t̂) ‖ ρ (384k + 32 bytes). Secret key dk = ByteEncode₁₂(ŝ) (384k bytes).

6.2 Encryption (Algorithm 14)

Encryption is the same trick with fresh randomness r: the sender makes their own LWE samples using the receiver's A and t.

y, e₁ ← CBD (from r), e₂ ← CBD fresh small noise u = Aᵀ·y + e₁ (k polynomials) ← transpose here μ = Decompress₁(m) each bit → 0 or 1665 (≈ q/2) v = tᵀ·y + e₂ + μ (1 polynomial) c = Compress_du(u) ‖ Compress_dv(v)

The message is hidden by placing each bit at 0 or at "half of q", then adding tᵀ·y, which looks random to anyone without s.

6.3 Decryption (Algorithm 15) and why it works

w = v − sᵀ·u m = Compress₁(w) is each coefficient closer to 0 or to q/2?

Substitute the definitions (t = A·s + e) and watch the big terms cancel:

w = v − sᵀu = (tᵀy + e₂ + μ) − sᵀ(Aᵀy + e₁) = ((As + e)ᵀy + e₂ + μ) − sᵀAᵀy − sᵀe₁ = sᵀAᵀy + eᵀy + e₂ + μ − sᵀAᵀy − sᵀe₁ = μ + (eᵀy + e₂ − sᵀe₁) + small compression errors └──── small noise ────┘

The large random term sᵀAᵀy cancels exactly. What remains is the message μ plus a sum of products of small polynomials. Each coefficient of μ is either 0 or 1665. As long as the noise is smaller than q/4 = 832, rounding recovers the right bit:

The probability that noise ever exceeds the threshold is the decryption failure rate. FIPS 203 gives about 2−138.8, 2−164.8 and 2−174.8 for ML-KEM-512, 768 and 1024. For comparison, 2−138 is far smaller than the chance of guessing a random AES-128 key on the first try.

6.4 Why K-PKE alone is not enough

K-PKE is IND-CPA secure (safe against eavesdroppers) but not IND-CCA secure (not safe against attackers who can send modified ciphertexts and watch what happens). Its ciphertexts are malleable: an attacker can change v slightly and observe whether decryption still gives the same result, learning a little about the secret each time. That is why FIPS 203 says K-PKE must never be used on its own. Part 7 fixes this.

The public key is t = As + e. The sender makes u = Aᵀy + e₁ and v = tᵀy + e₂ + message·q/2. When the receiver computes v − sᵀu, the big term sᵀAᵀy cancels and only the message plus small noise is left, so rounding recovers each bit.

Panel questions

Part 6

  1. w = v − sᵀu = (tᵀy + e₂ + μ) − sᵀ(Aᵀy + e₁). Substituting t = As + e gives sᵀAᵀy + eᵀy + e₂ + μ − sᵀAᵀy − sᵀe₁ = μ + (eᵀy + e₂ − sᵀe₁). The noise term is a sum of products of small polynomials, so it is small; rounding each coefficient to 0 or q/2 returns the message bits.

  2. Those two values are as far apart as possible on the "clock" mod q. That gives the largest margin (q/4 on each side) for noise before a 0 could be mistaken for a 1.

  3. Inside ML-KEM, the re-encryption check would fail, and Decaps returns the pseudorandom rejection key J(z‖c) instead, so the two sides would simply have different keys and the connection would fail. The probability is about 2⁻¹³⁹ to 2⁻¹⁷⁵, effectively never.

  4. So the terms cancel: the receiver computes sᵀu = sᵀAᵀy, and the sender's tᵀy contains (As)ᵀy = sᵀAᵀy. Using A instead of Aᵀ would leave a term that does not cancel. Our helper for this is mat_T_vec_mul_ntt.

  5. Without fresh randomness, encrypting the same message twice would give the same ciphertext, and u and v would reveal information. The fresh LWE noise makes (u, v) look random to anyone without s. In ML-KEM, r is derived from the message itself (see Part 7).

  6. IND = indistinguishability: an attacker cannot tell which of two chosen messages was encrypted. CPA (chosen-plaintext attack): the attacker can only encrypt. CCA (chosen-ciphertext attack): the attacker can also ask for decryptions of any other ciphertexts. K-PKE achieves only IND-CPA; ML-KEM achieves IND-CCA2.

  7. decrypt_noisy returns w before rounding, and bench/kpke_noise.py measures w − μ over 300 decryptions per parameter set. The largest noise was 345 / 284 / 236 for 512 / 768 / 1024, at most 41% of the 832 limit (Figure 6). A test also asserts the noise stays below q/4.

Part 7

ML-KEM and the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform

How a merely eavesdropper-safe scheme becomes safe against active attackers.

7.1 The FO transform in one picture

The Fujisaki–Okamoto (FO) transform (1999; the modern modular version by Hofheinz, Hövelmanns and Kiltz, 2017) turns an IND-CPA encryption scheme into an IND-CCA2 KEM. Its three ideas:

  1. Derandomize: the encryption randomness r is derived from the message itself, so encryption becomes deterministic and repeatable.
  2. Re-encrypt to check: after decrypting, the receiver re-encrypts the result and checks it reproduces the exact ciphertext received.
  3. Reject implicitly: if the check fails, return a pseudorandom key instead of an error.

7.2 The three internal algorithms (FIPS 203 Section 6)

KeyGen_internal(d, z) (Alg 16): run K-PKE.KeyGen(d), then build the decapsulation key:

ek = ek_PKE 384k + 32 bytes dk = dk_PKE ‖ ek ‖ H(ek) ‖ z 384k + (384k+32) + 32 + 32 = 768k + 96

z is a second 32-byte random secret, used only for implicit rejection.

Encaps_internal(ek, m) (Alg 17):

(K, r) = G(m ‖ H(ek)) shared key and encryption randomness, both from m c = K-PKE.Encrypt(ek, m, r) return (K, c)

Decaps_internal(dk, c) (Alg 18):

# src/mlkem/mlkem.py (decaps_internal, simplified)
m_prime = kpke.decrypt(dk_pke, c, p)
K_prime, r_prime = G(m_prime + h)
K_bar = J(z + c)                                   # fake key, computed every time
c_prime = kpke.encrypt(ek_pke, m_prime, r_prime, p)
if not hmac.compare_digest(c, c_prime):
    K_prime = K_bar                                # implicit rejection
return K_prime

7.3 Why re-encryption stops attacks

A chosen-ciphertext attacker tweaks a ciphertext and watches how the receiver reacts. Because r is derived from m, a valid ciphertext is completely determined by its message. Only honestly made ciphertexts survive re-encryption. Any tweak produces a mismatch and is rejected, so the attacker learns nothing from their tweaked ciphertexts.

7.4 Why "implicit" rejection

If Decaps returned an error on a bad ciphertext, the error itself would be a signal an attacker could exploit, including subtle signals like how long rejection takes. With implicit rejection, Decaps always returns 32 random-looking bytes. The attacker's key simply doesn't match, and the connection fails later in the protocol without revealing why. The key J(z ‖ c) depends on the secret z, so the attacker cannot predict it.

7.5 Input checks (FIPS 203 Section 7)

The public API adds validation before running the internal algorithms. Every failure raises ValueError in our code.

CheckWhereWhat it verifies
Type check (ek)check_eklen(ek) == 384k + 32
Modulus checkcheck_ekevery 12-bit coefficient in ek is below q: ByteEncode₁₂(ByteDecode₁₂(ek)) must give back the same bytes
Ciphertext type checkcheck_ciphertextlen(c) == 32(du·k + dv)
Type check (dk)check_dklen(dk) == 768k + 96
Hash checkcheck_dkthe H(ek) stored inside dk equals the hash of the ek stored inside dk

A tampered but correctly sized ciphertext passes the checks and is handled by implicit rejection, not by an error. The checks catch malformed inputs; implicit rejection handles well-formed malicious ones.

7.6 Internal vs public functions

FIPS 203 separates deterministic "internal" functions (randomness passed in) from the public API (randomness generated inside). Our public functions are thin wrappers:

def keygen(p):                 # Alg 19
    d, z = os.urandom(32), os.urandom(32)
    return keygen_internal(p, d, z)

def encaps(p, ek):             # Alg 20
    check_ek(p, ek)
    return encaps_internal(p, ek, os.urandom(32))

def decaps(p, dk, c):          # Alg 21
    check_decaps_inputs(p, dk, c)
    return decaps_internal(p, dk, c)

The separation is what makes testing possible: NIST's test vectors give fixed d, z and m, and we feed them to the internal functions.

ML-KEM wraps K-PKE in the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform. The encryption randomness is derived from the message, so the receiver can re-encrypt what they decrypted and check it matches. If it doesn't, they return a pseudorandom key J(z‖c) instead of an error, so a tampering attacker learns nothing. That upgrades IND-CPA to IND-CCA2.

Panel questions

Part 7

  1. To check the ciphertext was honestly generated. Encryption randomness r = G(m‖H(ek)) is determined by m, so re-encrypting m′ must reproduce c exactly. Any tampering changes c, the check fails, and the attacker gets no useful answer. This is what makes ML-KEM IND-CCA2 secure.

  2. On a failed check, Decaps returns J(z‖c), a pseudorandom key, instead of an error. An error (or its timing) would tell the attacker their modified ciphertext was invalid, which is exactly the information chosen-ciphertext attacks use. With implicit rejection, valid and invalid ciphertexts look the same from outside.

  3. A 32-byte secret random value used only to compute the rejection key J(z‖c). Because z is secret, the attacker cannot predict the rejection key. Our test test_implicit_rejection_depends_on_z shows that changing z changes the rejection key.

  4. Decaps needs ek to re-encrypt, and needs H(ek) to recompute (K′, r′) = G(m′‖H(ek)). Storing both avoids recomputing them. The hash check verifies they were not corrupted.

  5. It binds the shared key to the specific public key, so the same m used with two different keys gives unrelated results. It also protects against multi-target attacks where an attacker attacks many keys at once.

  6. Each coefficient in ek is stored in 12 bits (0–4095) but must be less than 3329. A malicious ek with values ≥ q is rejected. We test it by crafting an ek containing 4095, and 30 NIST "encapsulation key check" vectors test it too.

  7. We use hmac.compare_digest, which compares in constant time. But the choice between K′ and J(z‖c) is a normal Python if, and Python in general is not constant-time. Real implementations must do the whole selection in constant time. We list this as a limitation.

  8. In Kyber round 3, the shared key was derived with an extra KDF step over the ciphertext hash. FIPS 203 simplifies it: K comes directly from G(m ‖ H(ek)). FIPS 203 also adds the k byte into G during key generation and mandates the input checks. So Kyber and ML-KEM produce different bytes.

Part 8

Parameter sets and security levels

Three versions of ML-KEM, and what the numbers in each one control.

Setkη₁η₂dudvek (B)dk (B)ct (B)NIST category
ML-KEM-5122321048001,6327681 (like AES-128)
ML-KEM-7683221041,1842,4001,0883 (like AES-192)
ML-KEM-10244221151,5683,1681,5685 (like AES-256)

The shared key is always 32 bytes. The sizes follow from simple formulas that our tests check: |ek| = 384k + 32, |dk| = 768k + 96, |c| = 32·(du·k + dv). In our code these are the properties ek_size, dk_size and ct_size of the frozen dataclass Params in src/mlkem/params.py.

ParameterWhat it controls
kmodule rank: the size of the matrix and vectors. The main security dial (LWE dimension 256·k).
η₁noise width for s, e and y. ML-KEM-512 uses 3 (more noise) to make up for its smaller k.
η₂noise width for e₁ and e₂ in encryption.
du, dvhow many bits of u and v are kept after compression. Fewer bits: smaller ciphertext, more noise.

What the categories mean

NIST defines security categories by comparison with breaking AES: category 1 is at least as hard as recovering an AES-128 key, category 3 AES-192, category 5 AES-256. For key sizes of classical schemes with similar strength, NIST SP 800-57 gives:

Security (bits)SymmetricRSAElliptic curveML-KEM
1123DESRSA-2048P-224(none)
128AES-128RSA-3072P-256, X25519ML-KEM-512
192AES-192RSA-7680P-384ML-KEM-768
256AES-256RSA-15360P-521ML-KEM-1024
Common mistake

RSA-2048 is only about 112-bit secure, below ML-KEM-512. Comparing ML-KEM-768 with RSA-2048 is unfair to ML-KEM. Our charts pair schemes by security level, and we included RSA-7680 specifically to have an RSA point at the 192-bit level.

NIST recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default (FIPS 203 Section 8): category 3 gives a comfortable margin in case lattice attacks improve, at a modest cost. That is why our demo defaults to ML-KEM-768.

Panel questions

Part 8

  1. NIST recommends it in FIPS 203 as the general-purpose choice: category 3 (AES-192 level) leaves a safety margin against future improvements in lattice attacks, while its keys and speed are still very practical. It is also what browsers deploy (X25519MLKEM768).

  2. With only k = 2 the LWE dimension is smaller, so a bit more noise in the secret and error raises the attack cost back to category 1. The larger sets already have enough dimension.

  3. u has k polynomials compressed to du bits (32·du bytes each), v has one polynomial at dv bits (32·dv bytes). Total 32·(du·k + dv). For ML-KEM-768: 32·(10·3 + 4) = 1,088 bytes.

  4. Breaking it must require at least as much computation as a key search on AES-192, against classical and quantum attackers. It is a comparison-based definition, not an exact number of bits.

  5. About RSA-7680 (192-bit security per NIST SP 800-57). That is why RSA-7680 is in our benchmark. Its key generation took about 3.6 s, versus 0.08 ms for ML-KEM-768 in C.

  6. src/mlkem/params.py: constants N = 256, Q = 3329, ZETA = 17, a frozen dataclass Params with k, η₁, η₂, du, dv and size formulas, and the three instances ML_KEM_512 / 768 / 1024. Tests check them against FIPS 203 Tables 2 and 3.

9.2 The layer map

The implementation is built bottom-up, one module per layer of FIPS 203. Each layer only calls the layers below it, and each was tested before starting the next.

9.3 src/mlkem/: the implementation

__init__.py
5 lines

Marks the folder as the Python package mlkem. Its docstring warns the code is educational and not constant-time.

params.py
41 lines · FIPS 203 Tables 2–3

Constants N = 256, Q = 3329, ZETA = 17. A frozen dataclass Params (name, k, eta1, eta2, du, dv, rbg_strength) with size properties ek_size, dk_size, ct_size. Three instances ML_KEM_512, ML_KEM_768, ML_KEM_1024 and a lookup dict PARAMS.

hashes.py
42 lines · §4.1

H (SHA3-256), J (SHAKE256, 32 B), G (SHA3-512 split into two halves), PRF(eta, s, b) (SHAKE256, 64η bytes), XOF(rho, i, j, n) (first n bytes of SHAKE128). All use Python's hashlib. PRF and XOF check their input lengths.

encoding.py
117 lines · Alg 3–6, eq. 4.7–4.8

bits_to_bytes / bytes_to_bits (LSB first). byte_encode / byte_decode pack 256 d-bit values into 32·d bytes using one big integer (fast), plus byte_encode_ref / byte_decode_ref that copy the spec's loops exactly (used to test the fast ones). compress / decompress use integer-only rounding; compress_poly / decompress_poly apply them to a whole polynomial.

sampling.py
58 lines · Alg 7–8

sample_ntt(B): rejection sampling from SHAKE128 to make one uniform polynomial of Â, from a 34-byte input ρ‖j‖i. Asks for 504 bytes and retries with 168 more if needed. sample_poly_cbd(B, eta): centered binomial noise from 64η bytes; rejects wrong lengths and η other than 2 or 3.

ntt.py
118 lines · Alg 9–12

bitrev7, tables ZETAS, GAMMAS, N_INV = 3303. ntt and ntt_inv (7 layers of butterflies). base_case_multiply and multiply_ntts. Helpers used by K-PKE: poly_add, poly_sub, vec_ntt, vec_intt, vec_add, inner_ntt (dot product), mat_vec_mul_ntt (A·v), mat_T_vec_mul_ntt (Aᵀ·v).

kpke.py
96 lines · Alg 13–15

gen_matrix(rho, k) builds Â with the j-before-i order. keygen(d, p), encrypt(ek, m, r, p), decrypt(dk, c, p). decrypt_noisy returns w before rounding so tests and the noise experiment can measure the noise. Private helpers _sample_vec, _encode_vec, _decode_vec. All functions check input lengths.

mlkem.py
121 lines · Alg 16–21, §7.2–7.3

Internal (deterministic): keygen_internal(p, d, z), encaps_internal(p, ek, m), decaps_internal(p, dk, c) with re-encryption, hmac.compare_digest, and implicit rejection. Input checks: check_ek, check_ciphertext, check_dk, check_decaps_inputs. Public API with os.urandom: keygen(p), encaps(p, ek), decaps(p, dk, c). The parameter set is always the first argument.

oqs_backend.py
41 lines · optional

load_oqs() returns the liboqs Python module only if our own liboqs build exists (in Project/liboqs/install or $OQS_INSTALL_PATH); otherwise it returns None. This stops liboqs-python from trying to download and compile its own copy in the middle of a test or the demo. liboqs_version() reports the version.

9.4 One key exchange, traced through the code

  1. mlkem.keygen(ML_KEM_768) draws d, z with os.urandom → keygen_internal → kpke.keygen(d): G(d‖k) → gen_matrix (9 × sample_ntt) → 6 × sample_poly_cbd → vec_ntt → mat_vec_mul_ntt + vec_add → byte_encode(…, 12). Returns ek (1,184 B) and dk (2,400 B).
  2. mlkem.encaps(p, ek) → check_ek (length + modulus check) → m = os.urandom(32) → G(m‖H(ek)) gives (K, r) → kpke.encrypt: decode t̂, regenerate Â, sample y, e₁, e₂, compute u with the transpose and v with inner_ntt, compress and encode. Returns K and c (1,088 B).
  3. mlkem.decaps(p, dk, c) → check_decaps_inputs (lengths + hash check) → slice dk into dk_PKE, ek, h, z → kpke.decrypt → G(m′‖h) → J(z‖c) → kpke.encrypt again → compare_digest → return K′ or J(z‖c).

Panel questions

Part 9

  1. Eight modules, one per FIPS 203 layer: params (constants), hashes (SHA-3 functions), encoding (bytes and compression), sampling (matrix and noise), ntt (fast multiplication), kpke (the inner encryption), and mlkem (FO transform, checks, public API); plus an optional liboqs loader. Each module has its own test file, and each function's docstring names its FIPS 203 algorithm.

  2. Readability and fidelity: each line maps to a line of the standard, and there are no hidden vectorization tricks. Speed was never the goal of this track; the C libraries cover performance.

  3. byte_encode_ref copies the spec's bit-by-bit loop exactly, so it is easy to trust. byte_encode packs bits into one big integer, which is much faster. A test proves they give identical output for every d, so we use the fast one with confidence.

  4. It runs K-PKE decryption up to the point before rounding and returns w = μ + noise. It lets tests assert the noise is below q/4 and lets the noise experiment draw Figure 6. decrypt just rounds its output.

  5. keygen_internal(p, d, z) is deterministic: the same seeds always give the same keys, which is how NIST test vectors are checked. keygen(p) draws fresh d and z from os.urandom and calls it. Encaps and decaps work the same way, and the public versions add input checks.

  6. If liboqs-python cannot find the C library, it tries to download and compile it automatically, which would hang tests or the live demo. Our loader only imports it after pointing it at our own build, and returns None otherwise, so interop tests and liboqs benchmarks skip cleanly.

  7. About 640 lines across the eight source modules (the largest are mlkem.py with 121, ntt.py with 118 and encoding.py with 117). The whole project including tests, benchmarks and demo is about 2,800 lines.

Part 10

Testing and validation

How we know the code is not just working, but actually FIPS 203.

10.1 Four levels of evidence

LevelQuestion it answersExample
UnitDoes each algorithm behave as specified?NTT multiply equals schoolbook multiply
Round tripDoes the scheme agree with itself?Decaps(Encaps) gives the same key 300 times
NIST vectorsIs it exactly FIPS 203?240/240 official vectors, byte for byte
InteropDoes it work with independent implementations?our keys ↔ liboqs and OpenSSL, both directions
Why round trips are not enough

Two implementations with the same mistake still agree with each other. For example, swapping i and j in SampleNTT uses Aᵀ instead of A everywhere; keygen and encrypt both use the wrong matrix consistently, so round trips pass, but the bytes differ from every other ML-KEM in the world. Only fixed reference outputs catch that.

10.2 NIST ACVP test vectors

ACVP (Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol) is how NIST tests implementations for certification. Its public repository contains, for each test, the inputs and the exact expected outputs.

GroupCasesGivenWe check
keyGen75d, zek and dk byte for byte
encapsulation75ek, mc and K byte for byte
decapsulation30dk, c (valid and modified)K, including the implicit-rejection key
encapsulationKeyCheck30ek (some with values ≥ q)modulus check passes/fails as expected
decapsulationKeyCheck30dk (some with a modified H)hash check passes/fails as expected

All 240 passed on the first run, 25 per parameter set per group for keygen/encaps and 10 per set for the rest. The vectors came from NIST's usnistgov/ACVP-Server repository (downloaded through the jsDelivr mirror because raw.githubusercontent.com was blocked on our network; the upstream commit is recorded in vectors/SOURCE.md).

10.3 Interoperability

  • Seeded keys, byte for byte: given the same 64-byte seed d‖z, liboqs produces exactly our ek and dk (all three sets), and OpenSSL produces exactly our ek (768, 1024).
  • Both directions: liboqs/OpenSSL keys → our Encaps → their Decaps gives the same K; and our keys → their Encaps → our Decaps gives the same K.
  • Implicit rejection agrees: for a tampered ciphertext, liboqs returns the same J(z‖c) as our code.

Round-trip tests only show the code agrees with itself. We passed all 240 of NIST's official ACVP test vectors byte for byte and got identical results from two independent implementations, liboqs and OpenSSL, so our code implements FIPS 203 exactly.

It also produces byte-identical keys to liboqs and OpenSSL and interoperates with them in both directions.

  2. NIST's Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol, the system used to test implementations during official validation. Its public GitHub repository publishes test inputs with expected outputs, which we used.

  3. It uses fresh random bytes each time, so its output is unpredictable. The vectors fix the random inputs (d, z, m), so we test the deterministic _internal functions, which the public ones call. FIPS 203 separates them for exactly this reason.

  4. No, all 240 passed on the first run, because each lower layer had already been tested thoroughly (NTT against Appendix A and schoolbook, encoding against the spec-literal reference, the index order of SampleNTT, and so on).

  5. No. It shows functional correctness. Official CMVP / FIPS 140-3 certification also covers the whole module: side-channel resistance, key handling, self-tests and documentation. Our code is not certified and is not meant for production.

  6. From the mlkem folder with the venv active: pytest -q runs all 442 in about 10 seconds; pytest tests/test_acvp.py -q runs just the 240 NIST vectors.

Part 11

How we benchmarked

A fair comparison needs the same machine, the same harness, the same security level and comparable implementations.

11.1 Two tracks

  • Track 1, our Python ML-KEM: for correctness and understanding. Slow by nature.
  • Track 2, compiled libraries: liboqs 0.16.0 (C, which we built ourselves) and OpenSSL 4.0.2 through pyca/cryptography 50.0.1. RSA and ECC also come from OpenSSL, so the speed comparison is C against C.

11.2 Making RSA and ECC comparable to a KEM

Scheme"KeyGen""Encaps""Decaps"
ML-KEMkeygen()encaps(ek)decaps(dk, c)
RSA-OAEP (SHA-256), e = 65537generate key pairencrypt a random 32-byte keydecrypt it
ECDH (P-256/384/521, X25519)static key pairfresh ephemeral key + ECDH with the static public keyECDH with the static private key

11.3 Measurement rules

  • Warm-up runs first, then timing with time.perf_counter_ns and the garbage collector off.
  • At least N iterations and at least 2 seconds per operation (fewer for very slow RSA-7680 keygen: 5 per run).
  • The whole suite ran 3 times, samples pooled. We report the median (robust to outliers) and the IQR (middle 50%), not the mean.
  • Laptop on AC power, Windows power mode Best performance. An earlier run in Balanced mode was about 40% slower and much noisier (spread ~39% vs ~5%), so power settings are part of the method.
  • Sizes: ML-KEM raw bytes; RSA public key as DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, private key as DER PKCS#8, ciphertext = modulus length; EC points uncompressed (X25519 raw 32 B).
  • CPU cycles are estimates (median time × 2.4 GHz base clock). liboqs' speed_kem reported impossible cycle counts on Windows, so we did not use it.
  • Memory is Python-level tracemalloc peak only; memory used inside C libraries is invisible to it.

11.4 The machine

Intel Core i5-12450HX (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 12 threads), 15.7 GB RAM, Windows 11, Python 3.13.7. liboqs was built with MinGW-w64 gcc 15.2. On Windows, liboqs 0.16.0 enables only its portable C ML-KEM code, not the faster AVX2 assembly (that is enabled only on Linux/macOS), so our ML-KEM numbers are conservative.

Panel questions

Part 11

  1. We defined KEM-equivalent operations: RSA-OAEP encrypting a random 32-byte key is the standard way RSA transports keys, and ephemeral ECDH is exactly how ECC key exchange works. Every scheme does the same job: establish a 32-byte shared secret.

  2. Timing distributions have long tails: an occasional run is interrupted by the OS and takes much longer. The mean is dragged up by those; the median is not. The IQR shows how spread out typical runs are.

  3. That would compare an interpreted language against optimized C, and ML-KEM would look 40–160× slower than it is. For the scheme comparison we use liboqs and OpenSSL (both C). Our Python numbers are shown separately (Figure 4) to show how much implementation matters.

  4. With the final setup the median run-to-run spread was 5% and the median IQR 11%. RSA key generation is naturally noisy because prime search takes a random amount of time. The conclusions depend on orders-of-magnitude differences, which are stable across runs.

  5. Windows does not give reliable per-operation cycle counters to user programs, and liboqs' speed tool printed obviously wrong cycle values on Windows. We estimate cycles as time × base clock (2.4 GHz) and label them as estimates. Turbo boost makes the true count differ.

  6. RSA-7680 matches the 192-bit level of ML-KEM-768 and P-384. RSA-15360 (256-bit) key generation takes minutes per key, which is impractical to benchmark and not used in practice. That alone illustrates why RSA doesn't scale.

Our results, explained

Every chart from results/, what it shows, and the sentence to say about it.

All charts use the same colors: blue = ML-KEM, orange = RSA, aqua = ECC. On a log scale each grid line is 10× the previous one, so a bar one grid line longer is ten times bigger.

12.1 Headline numbers (median, microseconds)

ML-KEM-512liboqs C656725156

1,000 µs = 1 ms; 1,000,000 µs = 1 s. Full quartiles, run-to-run spread, estimated cycles and memory are in results/bench_tables.md.

12.2 Figure 1: key and ciphertext sizes

What it shows: ML-KEM objects are around a kilobyte. That is much bigger than elliptic curves (tens of bytes) and similar to or bigger than RSA. The secret key is large because it also stores a copy of the public key, its hash and z (Part 7).

ML-KEM's weakness is size: its keys and ciphertexts are about 35 times bigger than X25519's.

12.3 Figure 2: time per operation (compiled code only)

  • Key generation: ML-KEM-768 takes 77 µs. RSA-3072 takes 130 ms (about 1,700× slower) and RSA-7680 3.6 s (about 47,000× slower), because RSA must search for large random primes.
  • Decapsulation: ML-KEM-768 37 µs vs RSA-3072 decryption 1.43 ms (about 40× slower) and RSA-7680 30 ms (about 830×).
  • RSA encryption is fast (20–190 µs) because the public exponent 65537 is small. This is the one place RSA competes, and we say so openly.
  • X25519 is the fastest classical scheme (108 µs total), a bit faster than ML-KEM-512 (156 µs), but it offers no quantum resistance.

12.4 Figure 3: cost as security increases

What it shows: going from 128-bit to 256-bit security, ML-KEM's total cost grows only about 1.5× (156 → 242 µs). RSA key generation grows about 28× just from 3072 to 7680 bits, and P-curves grow about 44× from P-256 to P-521. At matched security, ML-KEM-768 is about 13× faster than P-384 and ML-KEM-1024 about 22× faster than P-521.

ML-KEM's cost barely grows with security level, while RSA and elliptic curves get dramatically slower. At 192-bit security, ML-KEM is about 13 times faster than P-384 and thousands of times faster than RSA-7680 key generation.

12.5 Figure 4: our Python vs optimized C

What it shows: our Python version is 36× to 158× slower than C for the same algorithm (ML-KEM-768 exchange: 13.9 ms vs 0.19 ms). Implementation matters as much as the algorithm, which is why the fair comparison uses C. Even 14 ms is fast enough for a live demo.

Where the Python time goes (results/profile_mlkem.csv, ML-KEM-768 keygen): CBD noise sampling 33%, encoding and compression 20%, matrix generation (SampleNTT) 15%, general Python overhead 12%, NTT 11%, NTT-domain multiplication 9%, hashing about 1%. Hashing is cheap because hashlib runs in C, while CBD loops over bits one by one in Python. In C implementations the balance is different: hashing (Keccak) is typically a large share.

12.6 Figure 5: the noise distribution

What it shows: our sampler's output matches the centered binomial probabilities (1, 4, 6, 4, 1)/16 for η = 2 and (1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1)/64 for η = 3. This supports Member A's math section: the noise has exactly the intended small, bell-shaped distribution.

12.7 Figure 6: why decryption never fails in practice

What it shows: the largest noise we observed was 345 (ML-KEM-512), 284 (768) and 236 (1024), at most 41% of the 832 limit. This is the picture behind the tiny failure rates of 2⁻¹³⁹ to 2⁻¹⁷⁵. Our experiment shows typical behaviour; the exact rates come from mathematical analysis in the Kyber/FIPS 203 documents, not from sampling.

12.8 Figure 7: bytes on the wire

What it shows: one ML-KEM-768 exchange sends 2,272 bytes, versus 64 bytes for X25519 (about 35×) and 806 bytes for RSA-3072 (about 2.8×). In TLS this can push the handshake over one network packet, which is the main practical cost of post-quantum security.

12.9 The four conclusions

  1. Correct: 240/240 NIST vectors and interoperability with two independent implementations.
  2. Fast: faster than RSA by orders of magnitude and faster than NIST P-curves at matched security; competitive with X25519.
  3. Big: about a kilobyte per key and ciphertext; bandwidth is the real cost.
  4. Quantum-resistant: the only scheme in our comparison with no known efficient quantum attack.

Panel questions

Part 12

  1. ML-KEM is faster than RSA by orders of magnitude and faster than NIST elliptic curves at matched security, but its keys and ciphertexts are roughly a kilobyte, about 35 times more data than X25519.

  2. Encryption (the "encaps" side): with the small public exponent 65537, RSA-3072 encryption took 37 µs, comparable to ML-KEM. RSA loses badly on key generation and decryption.

  3. X25519 is one of the most optimized primitives in existence, and our liboqs build used portable C without AVX2. With AVX2 (on Linux) ML-KEM is typically several times faster. Either way X25519 is not quantum-resistant, so it is not a real alternative.

  4. It must find two large random primes by testing random candidates for primality. How many candidates it tries is random, so the time varies a lot (our IQR was 80–100% for RSA keygen), and the cost grows steeply with key size.

  5. dk = dk_PKE (1,152 B for k = 3) ‖ ek (1,184 B) ‖ H(ek) (32 B) ‖ z (32 B). The copy of ek and its hash are needed for re-encryption in Decaps, and z for implicit rejection.

  6. It shows that in 300 decryptions per set the noise stayed below 41% of the failure threshold, a visual reason why failures are negligible. It does not prove the 2⁻¹³⁹-level failure rate; that comes from a mathematical analysis of the noise distribution, which you cannot verify by sampling.

  7. Python interprets every operation on individual integers. Profiling showed CBD sampling (about 30%, bit-by-bit loops), encoding/compression (about 20–25%) and matrix generation (about 15%) dominate; hashing is under 1% because hashlib runs in C.

  8. For ML-KEM-768, 1,184 bytes of public key in one direction and 1,088 bytes of ciphertext in the other, about 2.2 KB extra compared with a few dozen bytes for X25519. It is noticeable but acceptable for most connections; browsers already ship it.

Part 13

The live demo

What demo/demo.py shows, step by step, and what to say at each step.

Run it (from the mlkem folder):

source .venv/Scripts/activate
python demo/demo.py                          # ML-KEM-768, our Python code
python demo/demo.py --impl liboqs --params 1024
python demo/demo.py --fast --vectors         # skip mini benchmark, run NIST tests live
  1. Parameter set: prints k, η₁, η₂, du, dv, q, n. Say: "ML-KEM-768 is NIST's recommended default."
  2. KeyGen (Bob): ek 1,184 bytes (first hex characters shown), dk 2,400 bytes kept secret, time taken (about 5 ms in Python).
  3. Encaps (Alice): ciphertext 1,088 bytes and the 32-byte shared key K_alice in hex.
  4. Decaps (Bob): K_bob in hex, then a green KEYS MATCH ✔.
  5. Tamper attack: flips one bit of c. Decaps returns a different, random-looking key, no error is raised, and (Python mode) it equals J(z‖c′). Say: "Re-encryption detected the change and implicit rejection returned a useless key, so the attacker learns nothing."
  6. Use the key: AES-256-GCM encrypts a message with K_alice; Bob decrypts it with K_bob; the attacker's key fails with InvalidTag. Say: "This is what a KEM is for: it delivers the AES key."
  7. Mini benchmark: average keygen/encaps/decaps for ML-KEM-768 (liboqs and our Python), RSA-3072 and X25519.
  8. (Optional, --vectors) runs the 240 NIST tests live: "240 passed".

Panel questions

Part 13

  1. That is implicit rejection. Decaps re-encrypts, sees the ciphertext doesn't match, and returns J(z‖c) instead of an error. An error message would give an attacker information; a random-looking key gives none. The communication simply fails later because the keys differ.

  2. To show what a KEM is for. ML-KEM only establishes a shared 32-byte secret; real data is encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher using that secret. AES-GCM also authenticates, so the attacker's wrong key causes an InvalidTag failure.

  3. By default, our own pure-Python implementation. With --impl liboqs it runs the C library for comparison. The mini benchmark shows both, plus RSA-3072 and X25519 from OpenSSL.

  4. The public API uses fresh randomness from os.urandom for d, z (KeyGen) and m (Encaps) every time, as a secure KEM must. Only the deterministic internal functions give repeatable output.

Part 14

Limitations and security

What our implementation is not, stated plainly. Panels value this section.

14.1 Our implementation is not safe for real use

  • Not constant-time. Python's big integers, the % operator, list indexing, if branches and the rejection-sampling loop all take time that can depend on secret data. In principle an attacker measuring timings could learn secrets (a timing side channel). We use hmac.compare_digest for the ciphertext comparison, but the key selection is still a normal if.
  • Real example: KyberSlash (2024). Researchers found that several real C implementations of Kyber used a division whose timing depended on secret data, and showed it could leak the secret key. Even professional code can get this wrong.
  • No other side-channel or fault protection: no masking against power analysis, no fault-attack detection.
  • No secure memory handling: secrets are never wiped from memory, and Python cannot guarantee it (bytes are immutable; the garbage collector may leave copies).
  • Not certified: validated with NIST vectors, but not formally verified and not CMVP/FIPS 140-3 certified.

14.2 Limits of our measurements

  • One laptop; a hybrid P-core/E-core CPU adds scheduling noise.
  • liboqs used portable C on Windows (no AVX2), so ML-KEM's true best-case speed is higher.
  • Every measurement includes the small overhead of calling C from Python.
  • Cycles are estimated, memory is Python-level only, RSA-15360 was not measured.

14.3 What is not implemented

  • Hybrid key exchange (X25519 + ML-KEM-768 as in TLS) is discussed, not implemented.
  • No network protocol: the demo runs both sides in one process.

14.4 Security of ML-KEM itself

These limitations are about our code, not the ML-KEM design. ML-KEM survived six years of public analysis in the NIST process and is proven IND-CCA2 secure (in the random oracle model) assuming Module-LWE is hard. The main open risk is a future breakthrough in lattice algorithms, which is why hybrids and the conservative ML-KEM-768 default are recommended.

Our implementation is for learning and validation: it is correct, but it is not constant-time and has no side-channel protection, so it must not be used in production. For real systems you would use a vetted library such as liboqs, OpenSSL or BoringSSL.

Panel questions

Part 14

  1. No. It is functionally correct (240/240 NIST vectors) but not constant-time, has no side-channel or fault countermeasures, and does not wipe secrets from memory. It is an educational and validation implementation. Production systems should use vetted libraries.

  2. Leaking secret information through how long an operation takes. If a branch, table lookup or division runs faster for some secret values than others, an attacker who measures many operations can work backwards to the secret.

  3. A 2024 finding that several Kyber implementations divided a secret-dependent value by q using a CPU division instruction whose timing depends on its input. Measuring decapsulation timings could recover the secret key. Fixed implementations replaced the division with constant-time multiplication tricks.

  4. Rewrite it in a language with control over timing (C or Rust), make every secret-dependent operation constant-time (including the key selection in Decaps), zeroize secrets, add side-channel testing, and go through CMVP validation. In practice you would use an existing validated library instead.

  5. A major algorithmic breakthrough against Module-LWE, classical or quantum. None is known after decades of lattice research. Hybrid deployments (X25519 + ML-KEM) protect against this: the connection stays safe as long as either one holds.

  6. == stops at the first different byte, so its timing reveals how many leading bytes match. compare_digest always examines every byte, so its timing does not depend on where the difference is.

Part 16

Glossary

Every technical term used in this notebook, in plain words.

ACVP
NIST's Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol; its public test vectors are what we validated against.
AES-GCM
Fast symmetric encryption that also detects tampering. Used in our demo with the ML-KEM key.
Butterfly
The basic NTT step: combine two coefficients using a twiddle factor into a sum and a difference.
CBD
Centered binomial distribution: small noise made by subtracting two sums of random bits.
Ciphertext (c)
What Encaps sends back; it delivers the shared key.
Compress / Decompress
Keep only the top d bits of a coefficient to shrink ciphertexts; adds small rounding noise.
Constant-time
Code whose running time does not depend on secret values, preventing timing attacks.
CSPRNG
Cryptographically secure random number generator, e.g. os.urandom.
dk / ek
Decapsulation key (secret) and encapsulation key (public).
Domain separation
Adding a distinct label or byte to hash inputs so outputs for different purposes can never collide.
ECDH
Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange (P-256, X25519, …).
FIPS 203
The NIST standard defining ML-KEM (August 2024).
FO transform
Fujisaki–Okamoto: turns an IND-CPA encryption scheme into an IND-CCA2 KEM using re-encryption and implicit rejection.
Hash function
One-way function giving a fixed-size random-looking fingerprint of any input.
Hybrid key exchange
Combining a classical and a post-quantum exchange so either one alone keeps the connection safe.
Implicit rejection
Returning a pseudorandom key instead of an error when a ciphertext fails the check.
IND-CPA / IND-CCA2
Security against eavesdroppers / against attackers who can also get other ciphertexts decrypted.
IQR
Interquartile range: the spread of the middle 50% of measurements.
K-PKE
The inner public-key encryption scheme inside ML-KEM (IND-CPA only).
KEM
Key Encapsulation Mechanism: KeyGen, Encaps, Decaps; establishes a shared secret key.
Lattice
A regular grid of points formed by all integer combinations of some basis vectors.
liboqs
Open Quantum Safe's C library of post-quantum algorithms; our fast comparison implementation.
LWE
Learning With Errors: find s from A and A·s + small noise. Believed hard even for quantum computers.
Median
The middle value when measurements are sorted; robust to outliers.
Module-LWE
LWE where entries are polynomials and s is a vector of k polynomials. ML-KEM's hard problem.
Modulus check
Verifies every coefficient in ek is below q.
NTT
Number-Theoretic Transform: an FFT over integers mod q that makes polynomial multiplication fast.
PRF / XOF
Pseudorandom function (random-looking bytes from a seed and counter) / extendable-output hash.
Rejection sampling
Throw away out-of-range random values to keep the rest exactly uniform.
Rq
The ring of polynomials mod 3329 with 256 coefficients and X²⁵⁶ = −1.
Root of unity
A number whose n-th power is 1; ζ = 17 is a 256-th root of unity mod 3329.
SHA-3 / SHAKE
The Keccak-based hash family (FIPS 202). SHAKE128/256 are its extendable-output versions.
Shor's algorithm
Quantum algorithm that factors and computes discrete logs efficiently, breaking RSA and ECC.
Side channel
Leakage through timing, power use or electromagnetic signals rather than the math itself.
Test vector
A fixed input with its known correct output, used to verify an implementation.
